answers.java_tx_design: At the neobank, our core-ledger service does double-entry bookkeeping: every transfer between accounts must write a debit and a credit row atomically, and for years we wrapped that write together with a call to our notification service inside one Spring transaction, since it was simple and worked fine while we had under 50,000 accounts. As we grew past 400,000 accounts, our midnight standing-order batch, which processes maybe 60,000 transfers in a ten-minute window, started showing serious lock contention on the account_balances table -- I traced it with Postgres's pg_locks view and found transactions were held open for 200-400ms because the notification call inside them was slow and occasionally retried. My decision was to shrink the transaction to only the debit and credit write, which must stay atomic together for correctness, and move the notification into an outbox table written in the same transaction, drained by a separate poller. Lock hold time dropped to under 15ms. The failure that followed: under a later 5x traffic spike, the outbox poller itself became a bottleneck and fell eight minutes behind, so customers got transfer notifications late; I fixed that by sharding the poller by account-id range instead of running it single-threaded.
answers.java_ops: Operationally, the biggest problem I've owned was GC pauses on our transaction-processing pods once we moved to Kubernetes and started running four replicas under real load. We were on the G1 collector with default settings, and once daily transaction volume passed around two million, we started seeing GC pauses of 800ms to 1.2 seconds roughly every ten minutes, which was enough to trip our p99 latency SLO of 300ms for transfer confirmation. I pulled GC logs with -Xlog:gc and found young-generation collections were the problem, not full GCs, because our heap was undersized relative to allocation rate -- we were allocating a lot of short-lived DTOs per transaction. I increased the young-gen size, from roughly 512MB to 1.5GB of a 4GB heap, and switched our JSON serialization to reuse buffers instead of allocating a new one per request, which cut allocation rate significantly. Pause frequency dropped from every ten minutes to roughly every forty, and p99 pause length came down to under 150ms. It took two rounds to get there -- my first attempt was just raising overall heap size, which didn't help pause frequency and increased full-GC pause length when it did happen, so I reverted that part and focused on generation sizing instead.
answers.rust_readiness: I do have production Rust experience. About three years ago I built and now help run our risk-engine service, which scores every incoming transaction for fraud risk in real time before core-ledger commits it. We chose Rust because the scoring model needs to run in under 10ms at p99 including feature lookups, and our early Java prototype of the same logic was sitting at 45-60ms at p99, mostly from GC pauses interrupting a latency-sensitive hot path we couldn't tolerate pausing. The Rust service uses tokio for the async runtime and tonic for gRPC, talking to core-ledger over a synchronous-feeling request-response call that core-ledger blocks on before committing a transaction. In production it now handles about 300 transactions per second at peak, with p99 around 6ms. The failure I'd point to: about a year in, we had a memory leak from a cache we weren't evicting properly, which grew slowly enough that it took two weeks to show up as pod restarts from OOM kills, and I found it with heaptrack rather than anything obvious in our metrics. My view on migration generally is the same principle that got us here: cut a boundary where there's a real, measured problem, not because the language is more fun to write.
answers.rust_boundary: For our risk-engine boundary specifically, I placed it right before core-ledger commits a transaction: core-ledger calls out over gRPC with the transaction's features already assembled, gets back an allow/deny/review decision, and only then proceeds with its own commit. I kept the boundary narrow deliberately -- the Rust service owns scoring and nothing about the ledger's own consistency, so a bug in Rust can reject or approve a transaction but can never corrupt account balances, which live entirely on the Java side. Before migrating, we measured the Java prototype's p99 (45-60ms) and its GC-pause correlation with scoring latency spikes; after the Rust version shipped, we tracked p99 (down to 6ms), error rate, and, for about six weeks, ran the Java and Rust scorers side by side on shadow traffic to compare decisions before letting Rust be authoritative. About 0.3% of transactions disagreed during that shadow period, which we tracked down to a floating-point rounding difference in one feature calculation between the two implementations, and we didn't cut over fully until that gap closed to zero. If I were doing the ledger write path itself rather than a scoring sidecar, I'd apply the same shadow-and-measure approach, but I'd be more conservative about the boundary, since correctness there is much less forgiving of any gap.
answers.money_correctness: Every transaction that hits core-ledger carries an idempotency key made of a client-generated request ID plus our internal transaction type, enforced with a unique constraint on a transactions table, and any retried request -- from a client timeout, a mobile app resend, or our own internal retry after a downstream timeout -- gets the original result returned instead of a second debit or credit. This broke for real about two years ago: a partner payment provider we integrate with started retrying webhooks with exponential backoff after a change on our side slowed our webhook handler's acknowledgment past their 3-second timeout, and during a four-hour window before we noticed, roughly 1,200 webhook retries came in. Our idempotency key was built from the provider's own event ID, which we assumed was unique, but it turned out their retries sometimes carried a regenerated event ID after their fifth retry attempt, so 40 of those 1,200 slipped through as duplicate credits totaling about €6,800. We caught it the next morning through our automated reconciliation job comparing our ledger totals against the provider's settlement file. We corrected the 40 duplicates with reversing debit entries, not deletions, and fixed the root cause by keying on the provider's original transaction reference instead of their per-attempt event ID, since that field stayed stable across all of their retries.
answers.incident_response: The clearest incident I've owned end to end is actually the risk-engine memory leak I mentioned. Pods started restarting from OOM kills roughly every six hours, which wasn't originally alarming since Kubernetes just rescheduled them, until the restart frequency climbed to every 40 minutes over about two weeks and each restart caused a brief spike in scoring latency as a fresh pod warmed its caches, pushing p99 above our 10ms budget for a few seconds each time. I got pulled in when an on-call alert fired on sustained p99 breach, traced it with heaptrack over about three hours, and found a feature cache keyed by customer ID that we never evicted, growing unbounded as our customer base grew. I told the team in our incident channel as soon as I had a working theory, not after I'd fixed it, since others needed to know restarts might keep happening for another day while I built the fix. The fix was an LRU eviction policy capped at 500,000 entries, deployed within about six hours of the alert firing. The postmortem's lasting change was a memory-growth alert on all our Rust services, tuned to catch this kind of slow leak in hours instead of weeks; it's caught one other, smaller leak since, in an unrelated service, within about four hours of it starting.
answers.process_skipping: During the OOM-restart incident, once I understood the leak but before I'd fully tested the LRU fix, I was tempted to skip our normal canary rollout and push straight to all pods, since restarts were getting more frequent and I wanted the bleeding to stop. What I actually did was resist that and stick to the procedure: I deployed to one canary pod first, watched its memory curve for about 40 minutes against my prediction, confirmed it was flat where the others were climbing, and only then rolled out to the rest, which added maybe an hour of that pod cycling through a few more restarts than if I'd gone straight to all of them. In hindsight I think that was the right call, because my LRU cap number was a guess, and if it had been wrong I'd have wanted to know that from one pod, not all of them at once. I have skipped procedure exactly once, years earlier at a previous job, during a payment outage, and in hindsight I don't think it was justified -- the outage wasn't getting worse, I was just impatient. The bar I hold myself to now: skip only if measurable harm is actively growing, not just present, and even then announce it and get at least one other set of eyes before deploying, not after.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing early: about a year ago I pushed a config change to the risk-engine's feature-lookup timeout that I thought was safe, and it quietly increased our false-decline rate by roughly 0.4 percentage points for eleven hours before a product manager noticed customer complaints ticking up. Once I traced it back to my change, I posted in our incident channel within fifteen minutes of confirming it, named it as my mistake specifically rather than 'a regression,' and we estimated the number of wrongly declined transactions -- about 340 -- so support could reach out proactively. On-call and mentoring: I've carried on-call for the risk-engine and core-ledger, combined, for about six years across two companies, one week in four currently, and I still take pages myself rather than routing everything to whoever's more junior. I mentor two engineers who joined in the last year, one of whom I'm walking through their first on-call rotation next month, shadowing with me first. I don't think of any of this as beneath the work of designing systems; the on-call load is exactly what tells me whether a design decision I made was actually a good one once it meets real traffic, so I'd trust my own design judgment less if I'd stopped carrying a pager.
answers.evidence_decision: About four years ago, the team wanted to move core-ledger off Postgres onto a distributed database for horizontal scaling, arguing we'd hit a wall as account count grew. I disagreed, and spent a week benchmarking our actual write throughput against Postgres's documented limits, showing we were using about 8% of a single primary's write capacity even at peak, and that our real growth constraint was the midnight-batch lock contention I described earlier, not raw throughput. I presented that alongside a rough migration-cost estimate, and the team agreed to hold off on the database migration and instead invest in fixing the batch contention, which is the outbox change I made. I didn't quietly keep planning the distributed-database migration on the side; I dropped it entirely once the decision was made, and revisited it three years later, when account growth had actually caught up to a real throughput concern, at which point I was the one who reopened the conversation with new numbers rather than resisting it out of attachment to my earlier position. Separately, I've argued for and lost a case for rewriting a legacy batch-reporting job in Rust for speed, and once the team decided the reporting job wasn't worth the migration risk given how rarely it changes, I maintained it in Java without revisiting that.
answers.own_contribution: In the risk-engine work I described, the parts that were genuinely mine: choosing Rust and the tokio/tonic stack, designing the gRPC boundary and the shadow-traffic comparison period, finding and fixing the memory leak, and the LRU eviction design. What the team did: two other engineers built out the actual feature-lookup data sources the scoring model reads from, which I didn't design, and our data science team owns the scoring model itself -- I just serve it fast and safely, I don't tune its weights. For the core-ledger transaction-boundary work, the diagnosis and the outbox redesign were mine, but the poller-sharding fix I mentioned for the later 5x-traffic problem was actually built by a colleague based on a design doc I wrote, since I was heads-down on the risk-engine leak at the same time. I think it's worth being precise about that distinction, because 'I built the outbox pattern' and 'the team scaled it later' are genuinely different pieces of work, and conflating them would overstate what I personally did on the second half.
answers.java_recovery: Beyond the webhook-duplicate incident, there was an earlier case, about five years ago, where a bug in our interest-accrual batch job double-applied interest to about 900 savings accounts over a weekend because the job wasn't idempotent against being re-run after a partial failure -- it crashed halfway through Saturday's run, and our on-call at the time just reran it Sunday without checking which accounts had already been processed. I scoped the damage by comparing each account's accrual-log entries against expected entries for that date range, which is how I got the 900 number and confirmed the average overpayment was about €4.10 per account, small individually but real. I corrected it with a reversing accrual entry for each account, dated to the correction date rather than backdated, and I built a lock-based idempotency check into the batch job itself so a rerun would skip any account already processed for that date. I verified the fix by re-running the job against a full copy of that weekend's data in staging and confirming zero double-applications, then verified in production by re-checking accrual totals against expected interest for the next three weekends after the fix shipped, since I wanted more than one clean run before I trusted it.
answers.java_perf_change: On core-ledger, our account-history endpoint, which customers hit constantly in the mobile app, sat at p99 of 900ms against a target of 250ms once we passed about 400,000 accounts. I measured with a profiler and found the query was doing a full scan across a transactions table partitioned by month, joining across all partitions because our date-range filter wasn't being pushed down properly by our ORM-generated query. My first attempt was adding a covering index on the filtered columns, which helped average latency, roughly 900ms to 500ms, but didn't move p99 much, since the worst-case queries were customers with years of history and no date filter applied. The change that actually worked was adding a default 90-day window on the endpoint with an explicit 'load more' pagination affordance, which is a product change I had to negotiate, not just an engineering one -- most customers never needed more than that anyway, based on usage data I pulled first to justify asking for it. p99 dropped to about 90ms. The side effect: a few high-net-worth customers who did check years of history complained, so we added a separate, explicitly slower 'full history' export path for that minority case instead of optimizing the common path for their needs.
answers.rust_hands_on: In the risk-engine, the ownership problem that took me longest was around our feature cache: I wanted multiple tokio tasks to read from a shared HashMap of recent transaction features while one background task periodically evicted old entries, and my first instinct, coming from Java, was to reach for something like a mutex around the whole map, which worked but serialized every read behind the evictor, killing our latency target under load. I moved to a sharded structure -- effectively several smaller maps each behind their own RwLock, keyed by a hash of the customer ID -- so reads mostly don't contend with each other or with eviction on a different shard. The Send/Sync fight came later, when I tried to share a metrics-reporting closure across tasks that captured a non-Sync type from an early version of our metrics library; the compiler wouldn't let me spawn it across threads, and I spent a confused afternoon before realizing the library had a Sync-safe handle type I wasn't using, exposed under a different name than I expected. On async specifically, an early version of the gRPC handler accidentally held a lock across an .await point during a downstream call, which caused a deadlock under load that took me a day of tokio-console tracing to find, since it only showed up past a certain concurrency level.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move our account-history endpoint or most of core-ledger's account-facing read paths to Rust, even though they're the most customer-visible code we have, because they change constantly as product requirements shift and the team maintaining them is Java-focused; a rewrite there would trade measured performance for a maintenance burden nobody currently owns. I did hold back a real urge once: after the risk-engine's success, I wanted to also rewrite our legacy fraud-rules engine, an older rule-based system that runs alongside the newer model-based scorer, in Rust for consistency's sake. When I actually measured it, its p99 was 4ms with no real latency budget pressure, and its main cost was engineering time to maintain rule changes, which our fraud team, not engineers, edits through a simple DSL -- rewriting it in Rust would have meant either losing that DSL editability or rebuilding it, for a system with no performance problem. I raised the idea, measured it honestly in front of the team, and dropped it once the numbers didn't support it, rather than building a prototype first to make the case emotionally. My criteria generally: is there a real, measured latency or reliability problem, and does the team that owns the code's future changes actually want to own it in the new language.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Beyond the webhook-duplicate case, there was a settlement mismatch about three years ago where our daily reconciliation against a card-network settlement file showed we were short by about €2,300 across roughly 15,000 transactions for the day, which is small in aggregate but I don't like unexplained gaps regardless of size. I traced it by bucketing the mismatch by transaction hour and found it clustered entirely around 11 p.m., which lined up with the card network's own day-boundary cutoff sitting in a different timezone than ours; about 30 transactions near midnight our time landed in the network's 'next day' settlement file instead of the one we expected, so they appeared to us as missing for a day and then reappeared the next day as an apparent surplus. Once I understood it was a timing artifact rather than a real loss, I corrected our reconciliation logic to bucket by the network's day boundary instead of ours, rather than touching any actual ledger entries, since nothing was actually wrong with the money, only with how we were comparing it. My first hypothesis, before I found the timezone issue, was a rounding difference in currency conversion, since that's the more common cause I'd seen before, and I spent a wasted afternoon on that theory before checking timestamps.
answers.prod_data_verification: Yes, particularly with the risk-engine's shadow-traffic comparison I described: the honest answer is that comparing real transaction decisions between Java and Rust implementations meant touching real transaction data, and I handled that by making the Rust scorer's decision purely advisory during the shadow period -- it computed a result and logged it, but core-ledger never acted on it, so there was no risk of the comparison itself affecting a real customer, even though the underlying data was live and real. For situations where I couldn't get away with even that, like verifying the interest-accrual idempotency fix under real concurrent load rather than staging's much lower traffic, I used a masked copy of a weekend's real transaction volume replayed against a staging environment scaled to match production concurrency, rather than testing against live accounts. I have, once, checked a single live account balance directly, during the interest-accrual incident, to confirm my hypothesis about the average overpayment before writing the correction script, and I posted the specific account ID I was checking in our incident channel along with why, rather than treating it as routine. I don't think occasional, announced, read-only checks against production are the same as using production as a general test environment, but I do try to keep the bar for doing even that fairly high.
